source.title: An Empirical Study of Example Forgetting during Deep Neural Network Learning
source.authors: Mariya Toneva; A. Sordoni; Rémi Tachet Des Combes; Adam Trischler; Yoshua Bengio; G. Gordon

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study retrains classifiers after removing examples ranked by forgetting events and measures test performance, a different method for studying how training data affects generalization. Its results do not test the specific behavior named by any listed version.
record.gate_note: The study also reports forgetting-event distributions, correlations, and noisy-label results. These do not measure any listed version; cited results from prior work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study measures example forgetting and test performance after forgetting-ranked removal. Forgetting frequency does not measure V8's inclusion-based memorization score. Its experiments do not test any other listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate for the removal results. The authors additionally conclude that within-task forgetting occurs and forgetting statistics are fairly stable across seeds, training stages, and architectures. They interpret forgettable examples as possible analogues of support vectors; this is an interpretation rather than an established equivalence.
record.recipe_differences: The study ranks examples by forgetting events and retrains after removing them; it does not use the memorization-based criterion in V8.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and removal selection (forgetting-ranked versus random) change the reported outcome.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the least-forgotten examples preserves performance over substantial dataset fractions; removing equal-sized, increasingly forgotten chunks generally reduces accuracy, with a rebound at the most-forgotten end.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forgetting frequency identifies training examples with different contributions to held-out performance, allowing substantial removal of least-forgotten examples.

fits_no_version.finding: A WideResNet retains near-optimal CIFAR-10 performance after removing 30% of examples using a ResNet18-derived ordering.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Forgetting-based example selection can transfer between convolutional architectures.

record.problems: Several removal-sweep results are summarized in prose or figures rather than with exact point values in the text. The study's removal criterion is forgetting-event frequency, not V8's memorization-based criterion.

untested.parts: Near-perfect random-label fitting alongside natural-label generalization and chance-level random-label test performance; noisy-label forgetting distributions do not establish these outcomes.
Held-out error as width increases beyond the width required for zero training error.
Convolutional versus fully connected held-out performance and the contribution of local connectivity.
Controlled optimizer comparisons under limited or broader tuning; different architectures using different optimizers do not supply this comparison.
Batch-size effects under fixed epoch budgets and adapted training recipes.
Held-out performance with versus without dropout.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, its association with generalization gaps, and comparisons with other generalization measures.
Removal ranked by the effect of an example's inclusion on its own label prediction, compared with equal-sized random removal. Forgetting frequency is a different statistic.

record.verdict_notes: States are cannot_determine relative to the listed versions because no row measures their specified effects. This does not invalidate the reported forgetting-based removal findings. No verdicts are warranted.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Test error as network width increases beyond the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Adaptive versus non-adaptive optimizers and their held-out performance.
Large versus small batch sizes under fixed epoch budgets.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and its relation to the training-test gap.
The study removes examples ranked by forgetting events, rather than examples ranked by how much their inclusion raises the chance of predicting their own label correctly.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Retrained on subsets after removing examples ordered by number of forgetting events; compared with random removal and no removal.
rows.baseline: Base model trained on the full dataset; comparable generalization performance
rows.value: 30% of the dataset can be removed while maintaining comparable generalization performance as the base model
rows.note: The text reports this as a summary of the removal sweep; it does not give the exact test accuracy at this point.
rows.check: Valid removal result, but selection is by increasing forgetting frequency, not V8's memorization criterion. Specify that the least-forgotten examples are removed first.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Retrained after removing examples ordered by number of forgetting events; compared with random removal and no removal.
rows.baseline: Base model trained on the full dataset
rows.value: up to 35% can be removed with marginal degradation (less than 0.2%)
rows.uncertainty: mean +/- std error of 5 seeds (Figure 5 caption)
rows.note: The paper characterizes the remaining degradation as marginal; this is a different removal criterion from V8.
rows.check: The reported degradation below 0.2% is characterized as marginal. It does not establish an incomplete V8 effect because the selection criterion differs.

rows.subject: classifiers (architectures not stated for this aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Removed appropriately selected examples and retrained; reports the maximum removal fractions at which performance was maintained.

conditions.value: up to 80% of the training set

rows.value: performance is maintained after removing up to 80% of MNIST
rows.note: Aggregate statement; the main text does not identify the architecture for this MNIST summary.
rows.check: The architecture is stated in Sections 3.1 and 9: two convolutional layers followed by a fully connected hidden layer. The baseline is training on the full dataset. Figure 6 summarizes maintained performance rather than establishing exactly zero error increase.

rows.value: performance is maintained after removing up to 30% of CIFAR-10
rows.note: The aggregate Figure 6 statement is distinct from the ResNet18 results in Figure 5.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Retrained after removing increasingly large subsets ranked by forgetting events; compared with random removal and no removal.

conditions.value: all unforgettable examples (8% of the training set)

rows.note: The study says selected removal reduces the training set without affecting generalization; random removal drops performance faster.
rows.check: The maintained-performance finding is supported. The unforgettable fraction is 7.62% (3,809 examples), rounded to about 8%. Removal is based on forgetting, not inclusion-based memorization.

rows.subject: ResNet18
rows.operation_detail: Retrained after removing contiguous chunks of 5,000 examples with increasing forgetting statistics.

conditions.value: contiguous chunks with increasing forgetting statistics

rows.measure: Generalization error relative to a model trained on the full dataset
rows.baseline: Model trained on the full dataset
rows.value: Removing the same number of examples with increasingly more forgetting events results in worse generalization for most of the curve; the rightmost part moves up, suggesting some of the most forgotten examples actually hurt performance.
rows.note: The text gives a qualitative description, not pointwise values.
rows.check: Figure 5 right plots test classification accuracy after removing each 5,000-example chunk, not an error difference relative to full-data training. The qualitative trend is correctly described, including the accuracy rebound for the most-forgotten chunks.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
